slides.title: Overlapping calls require source-specific decisions
body: **Auditory scene analysis** is the organization of a mixture of sounds into representations of their sources. An **auditory stream** is a sequence of sounds perceived as belonging together over time. In a breeding chorus, recognizing a suitable mate requires a female to recover one male’s call from concurrent calls of other animals.

Nityananda and Bee tested Cope’s gray treefrogs, _Hyla chrysoscelis_, with an attractive pulsed target and a continuous sequence of distractor pulses. **Phonotaxis**, directed movement toward a sound source, provided a behavioral measure of whether the female recognized the target as attractive.

Target and distractor could each be audible while their combination disrupted recognition. Changing their frequency separation restored directed approach. Detecting acoustic energy and assigning the correct pulse sequence to a source are therefore different operations in the same listening task.

slides.title: Spatial separation improves frog mate recognition
body: **Masking** occurs when one sound reduces detection or recognition of another. **Spatial release from masking** is improved performance when target and masker come from different directions. Bee tested whether this spatial benefit helped female gray treefrogs choose the call of their own species.

Two sources of chorus-shaped noise surrounded competing conspecific and heterospecific calls. The calls were separated from the maskers by either 15° or 90°. The **signal-to-noise ratio**, or SNR, describes target level relative to background level; a negative value means the target is quieter than the background.

At −3 dB SNR, females chose the conspecific call with 90° separation but failed to make the corresponding choice with 15° separation. Source direction changed mate recognition even though the target call remained the same. Spatial organization can preserve species-specific information within a noisy chorus.

slides.title: Frequency differences separate concurrent frog voices
body: **Frequency** is the number of cycles of an acoustic oscillation per second, measured in hertz. A **semitone** is a relative frequency interval used here to vary separation between target and distractor. The experiment changed frequency while retaining the contrasting pulse sequences that identified the two sources.

With separations of 3 semitones or less, females responded weakly to the attractive target embedded in distractor pulses. Separations of 6–12 semitones increased responsiveness and shortened approach latency. The target became easier to recover as the competing pulse train occupied a more distinct frequency range.

The authors separately tested whether the frequencies were audible and whether females preferred the target pulse rate. Those controls establish that the scene effect involves concurrent-source organization rather than a simple preference for a particular pitch. Timing supplies call identity, while frequency helps keep the timing patterns separate.

slides.title: Group-flying bats increase differences in call identity
body: **Echolocation** is active sensing: an animal emits sound and uses returning echoes to investigate its surroundings. In a flying group, another bat’s emissions can overlap the focal animal’s echoes. Hase and colleagues attached microphones to individual eastern bent-winged bats, _Miniopterus fuliginosus_, to assign recorded calls to their emitters.

The bats produced **frequency-modulated calls**, whose frequency changes within a pulse. Their **terminal frequency**, the frequency at the end of that sweep, became more different between individuals during group flight than during solitary flight. Altering this feature reduced similarity among their emitted signals.

A familiar individual call structure can provide information for separating self-generated echoes from competing sounds. This sender-side adjustment changes the acoustic mixture before it reaches a receiver. It differs from a listener improving recognition of an unchanged target through spatial separation or neural filtering.

slides.title: Finch neurons preserve song patterns in a chorus
body: Zebra finches, _Taeniopygia guttata_, recognize learned songs against a background chorus of other finch songs. **Sound pressure level** measures acoustic pressure relative to a standard reference. Schneider and Woolley kept chorus level at 63 dB sound pressure level while varying the target song from 48 to 78 dB. Recognition declined sharply around equal target and chorus levels.

The authors recorded from successive stages of the auditory pathway. **Field L**, an early auditory forebrain region, supplied a relatively dense representation of sound. The **caudomedial nidopallium**, or NCM, is a higher auditory forebrain region receiving input from Field L. A subset of its neurons fired brief, selective responses.

These selective NCM neurons retained song-like response timing at background levels compatible with behavioral recognition. At stronger masking levels, their responses declined rather than becoming a copy of the chorus. Neural selectivity can preserve a vocal pattern instead of representing every component of the incoming mixture equally.

slides.title: Starlings report timing within interleaved streams
body: European starlings, _Sturnus vulgaris_, were trained to detect a time shift in a repeating tone sequence. The sequence contained A tones and B tones presented at half the A-tone rate. **Stream segregation** assigns alternating tones to different sources rather than treating them as one temporal sequence.

Itatani and Klump varied the frequency difference between A and B. Detecting a shifted B tone was easier when both had the same frequency than when they differed by 6 or 12 semitones. Grouping all tones together preserved a stronger local timing reference for the detection task.

Neuronal recordings from the starling auditory forebrain tracked the stimulus timing differences that predicted behavioral sensitivity. Here, separating streams made a particular task harder: recovering the timing relationship between tones in different streams. Successful scene organization depends on what information the animal must use.

slides.title: Wild caimans detect distress calls through noise
body: Female yacare caimans, _Caiman yacare_, respond to juvenile distress calls in their natural Pantanal habitat. Thévenet and colleagues played those calls against continuous broadband noise. **Broadband noise** contains acoustic energy across many frequencies and overlaps multiple components of the target call.

The call and noise speakers were either adjacent or separated. Females oriented and approached at less favorable SNRs when the sources were separated. The estimated detection threshold shifted from −14.6 dB to −18.2 dB, a 3.6 dB spatial benefit under field conditions.

Responses progressed from movement to orientation and substantial approach. Spatial separation improved access to a biologically meaningful signal without training the females to respond. The field recording connects acoustic source geometry to a natural parent-related behavioral response.

slides.title: Cricket frequency filters exclude competing sound
body: Tropical crickets hear calling songs within diverse insect choruses. Schmidt and Römer recorded an **ascending auditory interneuron**, AN1, in _Paroecanthus podagrosus_ and _Diatrypa_ sp. An interneuron integrates information from other neurons; an ascending neuron carries that information toward higher processing centers.

AN1 responded most sensitively near the species’ calling-song frequency. **Frequency tuning** describes how a neuron’s response depends on sound frequency. Sharp tuning excludes much of a chorus’s energy because sounds outside the effective frequency range produce weaker neural responses.

With target and masker on the same side, detectable signals averaged about −8 dB SNR in the laboratory. Moving the masker to the opposite side improved detection by a further 6–9 dB. Selective filtering and source direction therefore contribute separate benefits within the same identified auditory pathway.

slides.title: Young crocodiles use source position without training
body: Young Nile crocodiles, _Crocodylus niloticus_, produce contact calls that can elicit responses from other juveniles. The Crocoparc experiment broadcast these calls into a large outdoor basin while a separate speaker continuously emitted noise. Animals could move freely rather than being held at a fixed listening position.

The target speaker was either beside the noise speaker or spatially separated from it. Responses were more likely when the target occupied the separated location. The source-position benefit therefore appeared in a second crocodilian species and a different social context from adult female caimans responding to distress calls.

Untrained contact-call responses complement trained detection tasks. They connect spatial hearing to ordinary social signals, whereas a trained task isolates stimulus detection from the specific motivation supplied by a call. Both approaches test how sound geometry changes behavior.

slides.title: Frog lungs suppress frequencies between call peaks
body: The **tympanum** is the vibrating eardrum that transfers sound toward the inner ear. In frogs, sound also reaches its inner surface through air-filled pathways connecting the ears and lungs. Lee and colleagues measured these vibrations with **laser vibrometry**, which detects movement from changes in reflected laser light.

Inflated lungs reduced tympanic sensitivity in a frequency band between the two spectral peaks of the green treefrog’s mating call. **Resonance** is an enhanced vibration at particular frequencies; lung resonance produced a notch in the eardrum’s response rather than simply amplifying every received sound.

Deflating the lungs weakened this notch, and reinflation restored it. Calls of other frog species often contain energy within the attenuated band. Selective mechanical attenuation can therefore increase the contrast between conspecific call components and competing species before neuronal processing begins.

slides.title: A distinctive 2 kHz band protects katydid detection
body: Calling _Mecopoda elongata_ katydids overlap a loud, continuously trilling relative. Their signals share much of their frequency spectrum, but the chirping species has a distinctive component near 2 kHz. An **auditory receptor neuron** converts sound-related mechanical stimulation into electrical activity carried toward the nervous system.

Kostarakos and Römer recorded receptors tuned to different frequencies. Sharply tuned 2 kHz receptors continued responding to chirps during the competing trill, whereas receptors tuned to higher frequencies were strongly masked. The competing signal contained little energy in the frequency channel carrying the distinctive component.

The receptor terminals also occupy different positions within the auditory processing region. Frequency-selective peripheral activity can reach different interneuron branches instead of being merged immediately. A narrow spectral difference between two otherwise similar signals can consequently supply a reliable channel for detecting conspecific sound.

slides.title: Selective interneurons retain chirps during masking
body: The **prothoracic ganglion** is the neural center in the first thoracic segment that receives auditory inputs from the front legs. A **dendritic arbor** is the branching region through which a neuron receives synaptic input. A **synapse** is a junction at which one neuron transmits information to another cell. Several katydid interneurons extend dendrites into low-frequency input regions of this ganglion.

These cells were sharply tuned near 2 kHz and retained responses to conspecific chirps during a much louder competing trill. Selected interneurons remained responsive at SNRs as unfavorable as −21 dB. Their tuning and dendritic positions match the spectral channel that the masker largely leaves available.

Other recorded interneurons were broadly tuned and depended on adaptation to the repeating masker. The circuit thus contains two routes to selective responses: restricting the admitted frequencies and changing responsiveness according to recent stimulation. Both routes can preserve chirp-related activity within strong interference.

slides.title: A chirp recruits calcium signals in TN-1 dendrites
body: **TN-1** is an identified auditory interneuron in the bush-cricket _Mecopoda elongata_. Its dendrites receive input from auditory afferents, neurons carrying information into the ganglion. Bayley and Hedwig combined intracellular electrical recording with **calcium imaging**, fluorescence measurements that track changes in intracellular calcium concentration.

The researchers introduced the calcium-sensitive dye Oregon Green BAPTA-1 into the cell. A 280 ms conspecific chirp increased fluorescence in its dendritic field. The response reached its peak shortly after the chirp and then decayed over about a second, outlasting the acoustic stimulus.

Calcium therefore supplies a local cellular signal with a different time course from the sound’s individual pulses. The original recording follows this rise and decay in measured neural tissue. The extended calcium response provides a candidate link between recent acoustic stimulation and subsequent changes in neuronal excitability.

slides.title: ON-1 compartments retain different calcium time courses
body: **ON-1**, the omega neuron, is a local auditory interneuron that participates in processing the two sides’ auditory inputs. Its dendrites, **axonal branches**, extensions of the output-carrying projection, and putative **spike-generating zone**, the region where action potentials begin, can be measured separately within the same cell.

A 280 ms chirp raised calcium-sensitive fluorescence throughout these regions. In the reported preparation, the spike-generating zone produced the strongest response and the slowest decay. Approximate decay time constants were 0.7 s in axonal regions, 1.2 s in dendrites and 1.9 s near the spike-generating zone.

An **action potential** is a brief regenerative electrical signal transmitted along a neuron. Local calcium signals need not have identical amplitudes or durations wherever that electrical activity travels. Compartment-specific calcium dynamics allow recent stimulation to influence different parts of an auditory cell for different lengths of time.

slides.title: Different frequencies activate different TN-1 branches
body: **Tonotopy** is a spatial ordering of neural responses according to sound frequency. Auditory afferents in the bush-cricket ganglion project low-frequency information toward anterior regions and higher-frequency information toward posterior regions. TN-1 dendrites span these ordered input terminals.

Bayley and Hedwig presented 20 ms tones at 10, 20, 30 and 40 kHz. Calcium increases were strongest anteriorly for 10 kHz and posteriorly for 40 kHz, with intermediate tones activating central regions. These local signals reached their maxima within approximately 40–60 ms after the brief stimulation.

slides.title: Local estrogen synthesis alters finch song coding
body: **Aromatase** is an enzyme that converts androgen precursors into estrogens. **Neuroestrogens** are estrogens synthesized within neural tissue. In zebra finch NCM, this local synthesis can change during auditory experience, providing a biochemical route for modulating responses to vocal communication.

Fernández-Vargas and colleagues delivered **fadrozole**, an aromatase inhibitor, near recording sites while awake birds heard songs and song-plus-chorus scenes. **Narrow-spiking** and **broad-spiking** categorize neurons by recorded action-potential duration. Narrow-spiking neurons became less responsive and their response timing became less reliable. Broad-spiking cells lacked the same reduction in responsiveness to isolated songs.

Both cell classes nevertheless showed poorer song-like encoding within acoustic scenes during local inhibition. A biochemical change can therefore affect the organization of responses to mixtures even when isolated-song responsiveness is preserved in one population. Local modulation changes the neural representation available for distinguishing foreground song.

slides.title: Larval fish distribute auditory responses across the brain
body: Larval zebrafish, _Danio rerio_, provide optical access to activity across much of the brain. Poulsen and colleagues used **light-sheet microscopy**, optical sectioning that illuminates a thin plane of tissue, to record calcium-sensitive fluorescence while delivering controlled water-borne sounds.

A small speaker coupled to the chamber wall transmitted vibrations into the water. A hydrophone measured sound pressure and an accelerometer assessed particle motion. The stimulus set included pure tones, broadband noise and gradually changing sounds, allowing different response preferences to be identified.

Auditory-responsive neurons occurred in the hindbrain, torus semicircularis, thalamus and other regions. The **torus semicircularis** is a fish midbrain auditory processing region. Distributed frequency and temporal responses provide multiple representations of the same incoming acoustic stimulation, rather than a single undifferentiated startle signal.

slides.title: Marmoset recordings distinguish midbrain pathways
body: The **inferior colliculus**, or IC, is a midbrain auditory center receiving ascending information before it reaches the thalamus and cortex. Shaheen and colleagues recorded common marmosets, _Callithrix jacchus_, while they detected a target tone embedded in a sequence of noise sounds.

The researchers separated the IC’s central nucleus from noncentral fields using anatomical locations and physiological response properties. The central nucleus belongs to the **lemniscal pathway**, a principal ascending auditory route. Noncentral regions have different patterns of connectivity and sound responses.

The same tone and noise sequences were also presented during passive listening. Matching acoustic input across active and passive conditions separated changes due to task engagement from changes in the physical sound. Midbrain anatomy determined where behavioral state most strongly altered target-related activity.

slides.title: Mouse task rules change which sensory signal matters
body: **Selective attention** prioritizes information relevant to the current task. Morrill and colleagues trained mice to switch between auditory and visual rules while the same kinds of audiovisual stimuli remained available. Licking produced a reward only when the target defined by the current rule was present.

The sound stimuli were 1 s **tone clouds**, mixtures of brief tones centered near 8 or 17 kHz. Visual stimuli were moving stripe patterns of two orientations. Conflicting audiovisual combinations required the mouse to use the relevant modality instead of following whichever component had previously been rewarded.

The animals performed the task while running on a spherical treadmill in a virtual foraging environment. Changing the rule altered the behavioral meaning of physically identical sounds. This design isolates task-dependent sound encoding from a simple increase in acoustic level or a change in sound identity.

slides.title: Túngara frogs group components by relative comparisons
body: Túngara frog calls contain a **whine**, a frequency-sweeping component, and optional **chucks**, brief additional components that increase attractiveness. Female listeners must assign each chuck to the correct whine when several males call. A nearby component can belong to a different emitter from the loudest component.

Farris and Ryan presented multiple call components from different directions. Females favored grouping the components with the smallest relative spatial separation. When more than two components were available, their grouping depended on the relationships among the whole set, rather than an absolute distance rule applied independently to each pair.

The species-typical whine-then-chuck sequence also affected grouping. **Schema-based grouping** uses a familiar signal pattern as a template for assigning components together. Relative source positions and familiar call order jointly guide mate choices within scenes containing several plausible component combinations.

slides.title: Shared noise fluctuations improve frog recognition
body: **Comodulation** occurs when amplitude fluctuations in different frequency bands rise and fall together. Natural gray treefrog choruses contain this temporal relationship across parts of their spectrum. Lee and colleagues compared backgrounds with shared fluctuations, independent fluctuations and steady amplitude.

The synthetic backgrounds contained bands centered on 1.3 and 2.6 kHz. In the comodulated condition, both bands used the same fluctuating envelope; in the independent condition, each used a different envelope. The spectral bands remained comparable while their temporal relationship changed.

Female Cope’s gray treefrogs made fewer errors recognizing conspecific calls and choosing higher-quality calls in comodulated backgrounds. The auditory system can exploit relationships within noise itself. A predictable background structure can help recover a target even though the background continues to contain substantial acoustic energy.

slides.title: Crocodile training isolates sound detection
body: A **Go/No-Go task** rewards responding to a target while requiring the animal to withhold a response on other trials. Juvenile Nile crocodiles learned to approach a speaker after a synthetic buzzing sound. Using an artificial trained target removes the specific social motivation associated with a juvenile distress or contact call.

Continuous noise was broadcast from another speaker, and target location was varied relative to it. Separating the sources improved detection at unfavorable SNRs. The training experiment therefore recovered the spatial benefit observed with natural calls, using a different stimulus and a controlled response rule.

Across the field, freely moving and trained preparations, source position changed behavior consistently. The caiman field benefit increased with separation angle and became maximal beyond about 15°. Ecologically meaningful approach and trained detection provide complementary evidence that spatial geometry improves access to target sound.

slides.title: Cricket gain control reduces intercall background
body: **Neuronal gain** describes how strongly neural output changes with input. In the cricket experiments, activity evoked by the background was suppressed between conspecific chirps. The target pulses consequently stood out more clearly against the ongoing neural representation of the rainforest chorus.

AN1 recordings made directly in the nocturnal rainforest supported detection near −23 dB SNR, more favorable than laboratory playback of the same background. Multiple natural noise sources were distributed across space instead of being compressed into a single loudspeaker direction.

Sharp frequency tuning reduces admitted masking energy, directional hearing separates sources, and gain control improves contrast over time. These mechanisms operate together in one receiver. The natural spatial arrangement of the background changes the interference experienced by the neuron even when the recorded noise contains the same kinds of sound.

slides.title: A low-frequency component stabilizes katydid synchrony
body: **Phase locking** is a consistent timing relationship between a response and a repeating stimulus. Chirping _Mecopoda_ males synchronized their calls with conspecific playback even when a related species’ trill was louder. Males maintained synchrony down to −8 dB SNR with the natural chirp. When the 2 kHz component was reduced to match its level in the masker, synchrony broke down at +7 dB SNR. Removing a narrow spectral distinction greatly weakened timing coordination between males.

The first-order auditory interneuron TN1 also depended on this component for selective masked responses. Adding a 65 dB masker increased sensitivity to near-threshold 2 kHz tones by about 10 dB. Background sound can alter neuronal selectivity, rather than always producing a uniform reduction in target sensitivity.

slides.title: Local ON-1 signals support frequency-specific adaptation
body: ON-1 dendrites also express a spatial frequency map: lower-frequency tones recruit anterior regions and higher-frequency tones recruit posterior regions. Its axonal calcium response lacks this clear tonotopic ordering. Frequency information is therefore organized differently across compartments of the same auditory interneuron.

TN-1 and ON-1 showed frequency-specific response reductions, linking recent acoustic history to the channel that was repeatedly activated.

Removing input from the opposite ear increased ON-1 spiking and calcium responses and disrupted frequency-specific adaptation. Local cellular history and inhibition from the other side interact in determining which frequencies retain effective neural representation.

slides.title: Sparse finch responses distribute song identity across cells
body: **Sparse coding** represents a stimulus through activity in relatively few neurons at any one moment. In zebra finch NCM, broad-spiking cells emitted brief events at selected moments within particular songs. Different cells responded to different moments, distributing the song representation across the population.

During a 63 ms window, approximately the duration of a finch song note, fewer than 5% of the broad-spiking NCM cells were active. More than 70% of neurons in upstream populations were active over comparable windows. A selective population can therefore encode the temporal pattern while producing much less overlapping activity.

Background-invariant cells retained their preferred song events when the chorus was sufficiently weak for recognition. Stronger chorus levels reduced those events. This organization preserves a distinct vocal pattern within tolerable interference and reduces output when that pattern can no longer be recovered reliably.

slides.title: GABA blockade releases suppressed song responses
body: **GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid, is an inhibitory neurotransmitter. A **GABA-A receptor** is a transmitter-gated membrane receptor involved in rapid inhibitory signaling. Schneider and Woolley applied **gabazine**, an antagonist that blocks these receptors, locally near broad-spiking NCM neurons.

During blockade, cells responded more strongly and more song notes elicited spikes. Responses returned toward their earlier selective pattern after drug application ended. Inhibition normally limits how many acoustically relevant events produce output in these cells.

Presenting isolated notes also elicited responses to notes that produced little activity in the complete song. Earlier notes supplied a suppressive context for later notes. The pharmacological and context manipulations connect sparse coding to inhibition and recent acoustic history, rather than to an absence of excitatory sensitivity to the suppressed notes.

slides.title: Recurring sound sequences become auditory objects
body: An **auditory object** is a coherent representation of a sound source or recurring pattern rather than an isolated acoustic feature. Familiar patterns recruited sparser activity, reflecting learning of their recurring structure.

Neurons also distinguished patterns whose relevant elements were separated by an intervening element. This nonadjacent discrimination was stronger in the right hemisphere. Statistical regularities over time can bind separated sounds into a learned representation, complementing the immediate frequency and spatial cues that separate concurrent sources.

slides.title: Systemic estrogen inhibition alters female decisions
body: The zebra finch study paired neural recordings with an operant song-detection task. **Response bias** is a tendency to respond or withhold a response independently of how well the stimuli can be distinguished. Oral fadrozole increased response bias and reduced correct rejections in females, while males lacked the same behavioral effect. Local bilateral NCM injections did not reproduce that disruption. The location and route of the biochemical manipulation therefore changed the behavioral outcome.

Local aromatase inhibition weakened neural scene encoding without necessarily disrupting the learned choice. Systemic inhibition affected a broader set of aromatase-containing circuits. These results distinguish local coding changes from the distributed circuitry that supports an overt decision in noise.

Local aromatase inhibition weakened neural scene encoding without necessarily disrupting the learned choice. Systemic inhibition affected a broader set of aromatase-containing circuits. slides.title: Auditory attention reduces mouse cortical firing
body: The **auditory cortex** is a forebrain region that processes sound through interconnected layers of neurons. Morrill and colleagues recorded across these layers while mice used either the auditory or visual rule. Physically identical audiovisual stimuli could therefore be compared across different task demands.

Attending to the sounds reduced both ongoing activity and sound-evoked spiking. The effect was strongest in deeper cortical layers and in neurons without clear frequency-time tuning. Prioritizing auditory information did not produce a uniform increase in firing across the recorded population.

Sound classification from the neuronal activity remained accurate despite the reduced spike output. Selective attention can suppress activity that adds little useful acoustic information while preserving the representation needed to distinguish sounds. Fewer spikes can accompany more efficient encoding when their information is retained.

slides.title: Mouse sound information survives reduced spike output
body: A **neural decoder** is an analysis that estimates stimulus identity from recorded activity. In the mouse task, the researchers compared decoding from responses collected during auditory and visual attention. This tests whether a lower firing rate actually removes information about the acoustic input.

Accuracy was preserved when auditory attention reduced spiking. The pattern was particularly evident in deep-layer broad-spiking units. **Encoding efficiency** refers here to maintaining stimulus information with fewer spikes, rather than to a change in the physical energy of the sound.

Rule-dependent modulation extended beyond the trained tone clouds, changing the background state in which different sounds were represented.

slides.title: Prestimulus state contributes to mouse response changes
body: **Prestimulus activity** is neuronal firing before the sound of interest begins. Mouse auditory attention reduced this ongoing activity as well as the total firing measured during sound presentation. A response measured from zero includes both baseline activity and activity added by the stimulus.

When the authors subtracted each condition’s prestimulus firing, many apparent changes in sound-evoked rate became smaller. Reduced background activity contributed substantially to the difference between auditory and visual rules. The cortex entered the stimulus period from different neural states.

Attention-related suppression predicted correct performance during the auditory rule but not during the visual rule. The relevance of the suppression depended on which sensory decision the mouse was making. Neural state and task rule jointly determined how recorded activity related to the animal’s behavior.

slides.title: Marmoset engagement enhances target coding in midbrain
body: An animal’s **task engagement** is its active participation in the instructed behavior rather than passive exposure to the same stimuli. Marmosets detected a tone added to a reference noise. Single-neuron recordings measured whether the tone-plus-noise target evoked activity distinct from the reference noise alone.

In noncentral inferior colliculus, engagement preferentially enhanced the target response. This increased **neural discriminability**, the separability of activity evoked by different stimulus conditions. Noise responses were not amplified to the same degree, so the target acquired greater neural contrast.

Identical passive presentations controlled the sound waveform and level. State-dependent enhancement therefore occurred in a midbrain processing region before the auditory cortex. Auditory selection can alter subcortical representations as an animal performs a learned detection task.

slides.title: Central and noncentral marmoset fields differ
body: The central inferior colliculus is a major relay in the ascending auditory pathway. Noncentral fields include regions outside that central nucleus with different response properties and connections. The study distinguished these populations before comparing task-dependent changes in their firing.

Engagement had little effect on sound-evoked activity in the central nucleus, whereas noncentral fields showed stronger target-selective modulation. Applying a single state-dependent gain change to the whole midbrain would miss this anatomical difference. Behavioral relevance altered some pathways more strongly than others.

The result also differs from the broad firing suppression observed during mouse cortical attention. Both experiments used matched stimuli across states, but they measured different species, brain regions and tasks. Enhanced target contrast and reduced uninformative background activity are distinct neural operations that can support selective behavior.

slides.title: Marmosets interrupt calls when noise begins
body: Common marmosets use long-distance **phee calls**, tonal vocalizations that may contain one or several syllables. Löschner and colleagues triggered noise during ongoing calls to test whether monkeys could adjust vocal production after a perturbation had already begun.

Marmosets shortened or canceled calls after noise onset and produced longer calls after noise ended. The number of emitted syllables also declined during noise perturbation. Vocal behavior changed within an ongoing sequence instead of being limited to choosing a quiet time before starting.

The analysis indicated that some single-syllable calls had begun as planned double phees but were interrupted before the second syllable. Noise avoidance therefore affects both current sound production and the continuation of a planned sequence. A sender can reduce overlap by controlling timing and sequence structure.

slides.title: Bat terminal frequencies diverge within a group
body: Individual eastern bent-winged bats, _Miniopterus fuliginosus_, were recorded in solitary flight, group flight and another solitary flight. Returning to solitary flight supplied a comparison for changes specifically associated with the group acoustic environment rather than an irreversible drift across the session.

Terminal-frequency differences between group members increased during group flight. Other call properties, including duration and bandwidth, did not supply the same pattern of between-individual divergence. **Bandwidth** is the span of frequencies contained within a sound, distinct from the terminal value of its sweep.

The change emphasizes individual signal identity within overlapping emissions. A bat can alter its own output while preserving the basic form of its echolocation call. Such source-specific adjustment is complementary to a receiver suppressing background activity: one changes the mixture, while the other changes the neural response to that mixture.

slides.title: Onboard microphones sample a bat colony soundscape
body: Greater mouse-tailed bats, _Rhinopoma microphyllum_, leave caves within dense groups. Goldshtein and colleagues combined movement tracking with miniature microphones carried by individual bats. An **onboard recording** samples the sounds near the focal animal rather than only the sounds reaching a distant observer.

Conspecific interference was greatest during emergence and declined within seconds as bats spread through space. Movement data linked that decline to distance from the cave and increasing separation among animals. The noise encountered by a listener changed continuously during the same flight.

The original colony video records the dense emergence context, while the onboard waveforms measure each focal bat’s acoustic exposure. Together, these observations connect group geometry, changing interference and continued flight. A fixed external microphone alone would provide a different mixture from the one reaching the bat.

slides.title: Bats continue flying under rapidly changing interference
body: The onboard recordings contained intense calls from nearby bats during cave emergence. Pulse timing and acoustic measurements quantified the target animal’s own calls alongside these competing emissions. Tracking simultaneously measured movement through the crowded emergence area.

The bats continued maneuvering as acoustic interference changed sharply over the first part of flight. Their call parameters also varied with distance from the cave. The measured behavior provides a field comparison with terminal-frequency divergence recorded in smaller laboratory groups of another bat species.

The authors used a sensorimotor model to propose how spatially selective sensing and the timing of usable echoes could support collision avoidance. That explanation is a model-based hypothesis grounded in the recorded scenes. The original field video and measurements establish the crowded flight behavior; the model supplies a proposed mechanism for its persistence.

slides.title: Zebrafish neurons distinguish a broad frequency range
body: The larval zebrafish recordings detected auditory responses from 100 Hz to 4 kHz. Evidence of frequency discrimination extended from 100 Hz to 2.5 kHz. A neuron responding to sound at a frequency is different from a population carrying enough distinct activity to distinguish that frequency from another.

Frequency-selective cells occurred in several brain regions. Some regions grouped neurons responsive to similar frequencies in nearby locations. **Frequency selectivity** means that responses favor part of the tested frequency range instead of increasing equally for every sound.

This organization provides spectral information that could support more complex auditory behavior as the animal develops. The study’s direct outcome was differentiated neural activity, not a learned choice between overlapping callers. Fish auditory networks can represent multiple acoustic features before those representations are tested in a source-selection task.

slides.title: Fish populations separate onset, noise and crescendos
body: **White noise** is a broadband stimulus with energy distributed across frequencies. A **crescendo** is a gradual increase in sound amplitude. The zebrafish stimulus set compared these sounds with pure tones, brief onsets and frequency sweeps, rather than testing only whether an acoustic event elicited activity.

Functional clustering identified populations preferring a single tone frequency, broadband noise, sharp sound onset or a gradual crescendo. **Functional clustering** groups neurons by similarities in their measured response patterns. Cells could therefore differ in which temporal or spectral feature most strongly drove them.

The brain contains parallel descriptions of sound identity, change and temporal growth. These feature-selective representations provide the neural components from which a more complex scene representation may be constructed. The measured categories already exceed a binary distinction between silence and an undifferentiated acoustic stimulus.

slides.title: Acoustic signals also attract unintended frog listeners
body: **Multimodal communication** combines information across sensory modalities, such as hearing and vision. Their calls also attract potential blood-feeding parasites, creating interactions beyond communication with females.

Zhao and colleagues recorded midges approaching calling males and documented defensive movements used to repel them. Males performed arm waving, hind-foot lifting, wiping and limb shaking. Calling males received more parasite-related interactions and produced more defensive movements than silent males.

Some of these movements can become visual components accompanying the call. A signal’s recipients therefore include intended mates and unintended eavesdroppers, whose actions can change the sender’s behavior. The original video records the defensive interaction that supplies a possible origin for a multimodal display.

slides.title: Selected limb movements increase frog-call attraction
body: The torrent frog study compared audiovisual playbacks containing the same advertisement call and male appearance. Experimental versions added a particular limb movement; controls retained the call and male but omitted that movement. This isolates the effect of the visual component on female preference.

Females preferred combinations containing arm waving or hind-foot lifting, whereas wiping and limb shaking produced no corresponding preference. A movement that accompanies sound is not automatically an effective communication component. Its form determines whether it changes the receiver’s choice.

The authors hypothesize that conspicuous movements can alert a receiver to an accompanying call. The experiment measured increased audiovisual attractiveness rather than improved auditory masking thresholds. Multimodal enhancement and auditory segregation are complementary communication processes with different experimentally measured outcomes.

slides.title: Peripheral filters and central selection act in stages
body: A frog’s internally coupled ears behave as directional pressure-gradient receivers: external and internal sound pathways jointly determine eardrum vibration. Katydid receptor tuning restricts the spectral input reaching interneurons, and local adaptation changes the effectiveness of repeated frequencies. These mechanisms operate before or within early auditory circuits. They can preserve a target component without requiring the animal to switch an instructed behavioral rule.

Mouse attention changes recorded neural responses when the same sound acquires a different task meaning. Peripheral filtering, recent-stimulus adaptation and task-dependent selection therefore alter different stages of sound processing. Their behavioral benefits can coexist, but their experimental controls identify distinct mechanisms.

body: Gray treefrogs use frequency differences to recover an attractive pulse sequence from a competing source. Starlings separate interleaved tones, but that separation makes cross-stream timing comparisons harder. **Grouping** organizes sound components; its benefit depends on the information required for the particular behavioral choice.

Attention changes the relevance of an unchanged sensory input, while a marmoset can interrupt its own call when noise begins. Sender adjustment changes which sound enters the scene. Receiver selection changes how the existing scene is represented and used for a decision.

Torrent frog movements add a visual contribution to a call’s attractiveness without measuring an auditory masking benefit. items.text: Frequency and spatial differences help animals recover target signals, but their benefit depends on the recognition or timing task.
Directional ears, lung resonance and sharply tuned receptors alter target-to-background relationships before higher auditory processing.
Local calcium dynamics, frequency-specific adaptation and GABA-mediated inhibition shape which acoustic events produce neuronal output.
Attention and engagement alter target representation in specific cortical and midbrain populations, even with matched physical stimuli.
Bats modify call identity and marmosets interrupt vocal sequences, changing the acoustic mixture that receivers must analyze.
Detection, auditory grouping, selective attention and audiovisual preference are distinct outcomes; comparative claims preserve the task and measured response.
